query: Consider the following context: The recent perspective of multiprincipal element alloys (MPEAs), also known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs), has emerged as a very promising area for material design. Additive manufacturing (AM) strategies have also been noted to provide additional strength to HEA systems. In the selected dual-nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA system, an additional strength of approximately 300–400 MPa was achieved by adopting an additive manufacturing route as compared to its cast and wrought counterparts. However, the challenge of oxidation degradation always imposes a severe limitation for high-temperature applications in gas turbines, power plants, and aerospace components. Hence, ensuring material sustainability, longevity, and integrity for high-temperature applications inevitably requires the exploration of the oxidation behavior of alloys. In that context, which method can be used for elucidating the mechanistic aspects and elemental redistribution of nanoprecipitates on oxidation behavior, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In the dual‐nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high‐entropy alloy produced via additive manufacturing, high-temperature oxidation causes measurable elemental redistribution at the nanoprecipitate/matrix interfaces, which can be elucidated by Atom Probe Tomography (APT).
generation.material_initial_state: Dual‐nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA produced by additive manufacturing, featuring a nanoscale dispersed precipitate structure within a solid solution matrix.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to high-temperature oxidation conditions representative of gas turbine, power plant, or aerospace environments.
generation.conditions: Controlled oxidation at elevated temperatures (e.g., around 1000–1100 °C) for selected time durations to simulate service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoprecipitates and their interfaces with the surrounding matrix, which mediate oxidation behavior through compositional and structural changes.
generation.mechanism: High-temperature oxidation drives diffusion of key elements (such as Al, Ti, and Cr) leading to segregation and the formation of oxide phases at nanoprecipitate interfaces. APT’s near-atomic resolution enables detailed three-dimensional mapping of these subtle compositional gradients and redistribution events, thereby elucidating the mechanisms behind oxidation behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: APT analysis is expected to reveal statistically significant elemental gradients and segregation at the nanoprecipitate interfaces in oxidized samples compared to the unoxidized baseline, indicating oxidation-induced compositional redistribution.
generation.baseline: Unoxidized AM-processed HEA samples characterized by APT to establish initial nanoprecipitate composition and distribution.
generation.boundary: The observed effects are expected only under high-temperature oxidation conditions; variations in temperature, time or alloy processing may influence the magnitude and nature of the elemental redistribution.
generation.uncertainty: While APT is capable of revealing nanoscale compositional changes, the exact magnitude of elemental redistribution and its quantitative correlation to oxidation resistance remain uncertain until experimentally quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AM-processed dual-nanoprecipitation HEA samples. First, perform baseline APT characterization on one set to document the initial three-dimensional compositional mapping of nanoprecipitates. Second, expose the other set to controlled high-temperature oxidation (e.g., 1000–1100 °C for predetermined durations). Post-oxidation, perform APT analysis on these samples and quantitatively compare the elemental distributions, especially at the nanoprecipitate/matrix interfaces, to the baseline measurements.
measurements: Elemental concentration profiles across nanoprecipitate interfaces
Comparative analysis of oxide phase formation (optionally via TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If APT data do not show statistically significant differences or consistent trends in elemental redistribution (e.g., segregation or depletion at the nanoprecipitate interfaces) between the oxidized and baseline samples, then the hypothesis that high-temperature oxidation engenders detectable elemental redistribution in this HEA will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEA, also called multi‐principal‐element refractory alloys) comprise five or more principal elements from the refractory transition metals (group 4–6 elements: Zr, Hf, V, Nb, Ta, Mo, and W, often with Ti and Cr also considered), [ [1] , [2] , [3] ] with structural applications under extreme temperature conditions, beyond those where nickel‐based superalloys can be used. [ [4] ] Additive manufacturing (AM) of RHEAs can facilitate the exploration of possible applications for RHEA via rapid prototyping of parts with complex shapes with high powder feedstock utilization. Recently, laser melting deposition (LMD) was used to fabricate NbTaTiZr, [ [5] ] HfNbTiZr, [ [6] ] HfNbTaTiZr, [ [7] , [8] ] and MoNbTaW [ [9] , [10] , [11] ] quaternary and quinary refractory concentrated alloys. However, the feature resolution of LMD is relatively low, as the size of the melt pool is as large as ≈3 mm. [ [7] , [8] ] In addition, no complex parts have been demonstrated for these refractory alloys by using LMD.
